screens.title: High Availability & Fault Tolerance Strategies
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we focus on practical patterns that keep applications running when things fail. You will learn the difference between high availability and fault tolerance, and why both matter when architecting for production workloads. We will explore how Availability Zones and Regions form the physical foundation of resilience, and how services like Elastic Load Balancing and Auto Scaling create self-healing front doors and horizontally scaled fleets. You will also walk through common disaster recovery strategies — backup and restore, pilot light, warm standby, and multi-site active/active — and learn to match each to Recovery Time Objectives and Recovery Point Objectives. Finally, we will highlight typical single points of failure you must eliminate, such as single-instance databases or missing cross-AZ replication, and the simple changes that reduce risk. By the end of this lesson you will be able to propose a multi-AZ design for a simple web application, choose an appropriate DR pattern for business requirements, and identify where redundancy is missing. Think about a legacy app you know: how quickly could it recover from an AZ outage, and what would you change first?

Module 8 › Chapter 8.1 › Overview
High Availability & Fault Tolerance Strategies
Design resilient AWS systems that remain operational and recover automatically.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will do four practical things that improve system resilience. First, you will clearly explain how high availability differs from fault tolerance and why both are needed for critical services. Second, you will design multi-Availability Zone and multi-Region layouts that reduce the blast radius of failures and support business continuity. Third, you will configure and reason about Application Load Balancers and Auto Scaling Groups so your application can route around unhealthy instances and replace failed capacity automatically. Fourth, you will choose and justify a disaster recovery pattern — backup and restore, pilot light, warm standby, or multi-site active/active — based on Recovery Time Objective and Recovery Point Objective targets. Each objective focuses on practical decision-making and hands-on skills that map directly to real AWS deployments and exams. As you progress, think about which objective you would practice first on a test application and why.

screens.title: High Availability vs Fault Tolerance
screens.narratorSegment: High availability and fault tolerance are related goals but they are not the same. High availability focuses on keeping a system operational for a long time and is often expressed as an uptime percentage — for example, 99.99 percent availability. Achieving HA means designing to reduce downtime through redundancy, fast detection, and quick recovery. Fault tolerance is a stronger claim: the system continues operating without interruption even when one or more components fail. True fault-tolerant systems mask failures so users notice no downtime at all. In practice you choose a mix: multi-AZ deployments and load balancers provide high availability by keeping services running despite component failures, while synchronous replication and active/active multi-Region architectures approach fault tolerance by eliminating single failure modes. A common misconception is that adding more instances alone guarantees fault tolerance. It does not unless you also eliminate correlated failure modes like a single database or single NAT gateway. Example: deploying two identical web servers in a single AZ behind a load balancer improves availability against instance failure, but won’t protect you if the AZ loses power. The takeaway: map business availability targets to design choices and then remove single points of failure methodically.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.1 › HA vs Fault Tolerance
Definition
Clear claims and expectations
High Availability
A design goal to minimize downtime and meet uptime percentages; uses redundancy and rapid recovery.
Fault Tolerance
A stronger claim to continue operating without interruption despite component failures; often costly and complex.
Key Takeaway

Match availability goals to design choices: redundancy and fast recovery for HA; masking and duplication for fault tolerance.

Concrete example
Two web servers in a single AZ vs two servers in two AZs:
  • Same AZ: survives one instance failure, but vulnerable to AZ outage.
  • Multi-AZ: survives instance failure and AZ failure, improving availability significantly.
Common misconception
More instances alone do not eliminate correlated failures like single databases, single NAT gateways, or single-region dependencies.
Reflection
Which component in your current design would cause the entire system to fail if it stopped working? Plan one redundancy for it.

screens.title: Regions and Availability Zones
screens.narratorSegment: Regions and Availability Zones are the physical building blocks for resilience on AWS. A Region represents a geographic area containing multiple isolated AZs. An AZ is one or more discrete data centers with independent power and networking. Because AZs within a Region are interconnected using high-bandwidth, low-latency links, you can run multi-AZ architectures that replicate data and route traffic between AZs quickly. Deploying application tiers — web, application, and database — across multiple AZs reduces the impact of a single data center failure. For example, running two web server instances in different AZs behind an Application Load Balancer means the ALB will route traffic to the healthy instance if the other AZ fails. Extending resilience across Regions protects against larger disasters, but introduces replication complexity and possible cross-Region latency. A practical trade-off is to use multi-AZ within a Region for typical HA needs and reserve multi-Region designs for critical services with near-zero RTO requirements. Misconception: AZs are backups of each other; they are independent sites and require explicit replication or multi-AZ managed services to replicate state. Consider where to place stateful components and prefer managed multi-AZ options when possible.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.1 › Regions & AZs
Physical separation
Regions contain multiple AZs. AZs are isolated data centers with redundant power and networking.
AZ interconnect
High-bandwidth, low-latency links allow synchronous replication and fast failover within a Region.
Multi-Region trade-offs
Multi-Region gives highest fault tolerance but adds complexity and potential latency for cross-Region replication.
Practical rule

Prefer multi-AZ for most production systems. Reserve multi-Region for business-critical services that must survive regional disasters.

Concrete scenario
A web app deployed in two AZs with an ALB and RDS Multi-AZ will survive a single AZ outage with minimal downtime. If your app requires near-zero downtime even for Region failures, plan multi-Region active/active and accept complexity in data replication and DNS failover.
Misconception check
AZs are not automatic backups; you must deploy resources across AZs or use managed multi-AZ services to gain redundancy.
Visualization: imagine Regions as cities and AZs as separate buildings inside the city. Losing a building shouldn’t close the city if services are spread across buildings.

screens.title: Elastic Load Balancing types and behavior
screens.narratorSegment: Elastic Load Balancing provides managed entry points that distribute traffic to multiple targets and remove unhealthy targets automatically. There are three primary types. Application Load Balancer is optimized for HTTP and HTTPS and supports path-based routing, host-based routing, and advanced request processing. Use ALB when you need layer 7 features for web applications. Network Load Balancer operates at layer 4 and is designed for extreme performance and low latency for TCP, UDP, or TLS traffic. It preserves source IP and is a good fit for performance-sensitive or non-HTTP workloads. Gateway Load Balancer is used for routing traffic to third-party virtual appliances, like firewalls, without changing your networking. Health checks are critical: ELB will detect an unhealthy instance and stop sending traffic to it, preventing requests from hitting failed nodes and eliminating the load balancer itself as a single point of failure. A common misconception is that the presence of a load balancer alone fixes stateful backend issues; it only routes and checks health. If your backend stores state locally on instances, replacing an instance won't restore state. Example: use ALB with an ASG and stateless web servers that store session state in a shared cache or database. The key takeaway: pick the right balancer type and use health checks plus stateless designs to reap HA benefits.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.1 › Elastic Load Balancing
Load balancer comparison
Application Load Balancer (ALB)
Layer 7 routing for HTTP/HTTPS, host/path rules, and web application use cases.
Network Load Balancer (NLB)
Layer 4 performance for TCP/UDP with preserved source IP and very low latency.
Gateway Load Balancer (GWLB)
Routes to third-party virtual appliances for inspection or filtering.
Health checks and state
ELB health checks stop sending traffic to unhealthy targets. Combine health checks with stateless service design so replacements can serve traffic immediately.
Concrete example
ALB with target group across two AZs and ASG running stateless web servers; session state stored in a shared cache or database to avoid lost sessions when instances rotate.
Key Takeaway

Choose the ELB type based on protocol and features, and use health checks plus stateless design to remove single points of failure.

screens.title: Auto Scaling Groups and self-healing
screens.narratorSegment: Auto Scaling Groups maintain the desired number of instances for a logical group and provide self-healing behavior. An ASG watches instance health using ELB or EC2 health checks and will terminate and replace instances that fail. Scaling policies — scheduled, simple, or target-tracking — allow ASGs to respond to demand changes automatically. The typical process is: define a launch template or launch configuration that contains the AMI, instance type, and user data; create an ASG with desired/min/max capacity and configure health checks; attach the ASG to a target group on an Application Load Balancer so ELB health checks can inform ASG decisions. Example: set desired capacity to two across two AZs and attach an ALB. If C P U spikes, target tracking can scale out to meet load. If an instance becomes unhealthy, the ASG terminates it and launches a replacement using the same launch template, preserving desired capacity and reducing manual intervention. Common misconception: ASG protects only compute, not configuration drift. Ensure your launch template contains all bootstrapping (user data or configuration management) so replacements are identical. The practical takeaway is to treat ASG as the fundamental mechanism for horizontal resilience and combine it with stateless services and externalized state for fast recovery.

keyIdea.title: ASG pattern
keyIdea.text: Use a launch template, attach ASG to ELB, and rely on health checks and scaling policies to maintain capacity and respond to demand or failures.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.1 › Auto Scaling Groups
ASG lifecycle
Launch template → ASG configuration → health checks → replace or scale.
Step 1: Create Launch Template
Include AMI, instance type, security groups, and user data to bootstrap the instance.
Step 2: Define ASG
Set desired, min, and max capacity and select AZ subnets.
Step 3: Attach to ALB
Use target groups and ELB health checks so ASG knows which instances serve traffic.
Concrete example
Desired capacity 2 across two AZs. If one instance fails, the ASG launches a replacement using the launch template and the ALB stops routing to the unhealthy instance.
Misconception
ASG replaces instances but will not fix broken bootstrapping. Ensure user data and configuration management are correct so replacements are healthy out of the box.
Key Takeaway

ASG plus ELB provides self-healing compute fleets. Keep instances stateless and bootstrap fully so replacements are reliable.

screens.title: Disaster Recovery strategies and RTO/RPO
screens.narratorSegment: Disaster recovery strategies trade cost and complexity for lower Recovery Time Objective and Recovery Point Objective. RTO is the maximum acceptable delay to restore service after an outage; RPO is the maximum acceptable amount of data loss measured in time. The simplest DR approach, Backup and Restore, periodically saves data and recreates environments when needed. It has high RTO and RPO — recovery can take hours or longer and recent data may be lost. Pilot Light keeps a minimal set of core services and replicated data running in a DR Region. It reduces RTO and RPO because only full capacity needs to be scaled up after a disaster. Warm Standby maintains a scaled-down but functional environment that can be quickly scaled to production capacity, lowering RTO/RPO further at higher cost. Multi-Site Active/Active runs the application in multiple Regions simultaneously, often providing near-zero RTO and RPO but incurring the highest cost and complexity for data consistency and traffic routing. Example decision: if your business requires recovery within a few hours and can tolerate limited recent data loss, Pilot Light is cost-effective. If you need continuous operation with minimal data loss, invest in active/active. Always test your chosen strategy — untested DR is not a plan. Run drills, measure actual RTO/RPO, and adjust architecture and runbooks accordingly.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.1 › Disaster Recovery
DR strategies mapped to RTO/RPO
A timeline view of cost, complexity, and recovery guarantees.
Backup & Restore
Lowest cost, highest RTO/RPO. Restore from backups when disaster occurs.
Pilot Light
Core services and data replicated; scale up on demand. Lower RTO/RPO than backup/restore.
Warm Standby
Scaled-down but functional environment running continuously; quick to scale to full capacity.
Multi-Site Active/Active
Active in multiple Regions simultaneously; lowest RTO/RPO but highest cost and complexity.
Example decision

Given RPO 4 hours and RTO 8 hours, a Pilot Light strategy balances cost and recovery time and is often the most appropriate choice.

Warning

An untested DR plan will likely fail in a real disaster. Run regular drills and measure actual recovery times.

screens.title: Launch Template user-data (bootstrapping)
screens.narratorSegment: Bootstrapping instances with user data is essential so Auto Scaling Group replacements come online healthy and consistent. The user data script installs and starts Apache, enables the service, and writes a simple web page that includes the instance ID and Availability Zone — a helpful verification step. In this example the script updates packages, installs the web server, starts it, and writes an index. html that prints the instance metadata for the instance ID and AZ. A common mistake is to omit error handling or assume network access during boot. If a package repository is unreachable, the instance will be unhealthy. Also, long-running bootstrap steps can delay health checks; prefer fast, idempotent scripts and pull large assets from a pre-baked AMI when possible. Example verification: after ASG launches instances across two AZs, visit the ALB DNS and refresh to observe different instance IDs and AZs in the page. This demonstrates that instances are provisioned correctly and that the ALB distributes traffic. Keep your launch template immutable so replacement instances use the same bootstrapping behavior consistently. Launch Template user-data (bootstrapping) means put repeatable provisioning in user data or a baked ami so asg replacements are consistent and pass health checks quickly.. In practical terms, use user-data to provision a simple apache web server for asg instances. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.1 › Launch Template User Data
User-data bootstrapping script
This script installs Apache and writes a page that reveals the instance ID and AZ for verification.
#!/bin/bash
yum update -y
yum install -y httpd
systemctl start httpd
systemctl enable httpd
EC2_INSTANCE_ID=$(curl -s http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/instance-id)
EC2_AZ=$(curl -s http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/placement/availability-zone)
echo "<h1>Hello from instance $EC2_INSTANCE_ID in AZ $EC2_AZ</h1>" > /var/www/html/index.html
Bootstrapping tips
  • Keep scripts idempotent and fast so health checks can pass quickly.
  • Prefer pre-baked AMIs for large dependencies to reduce boot time.
  • Log bootstrap progress to enable debugging when instances fail health checks.
Verification
Open the ALB DNS and refresh. You should see different instance IDs and AZ names on successive requests, showing that the ALB balances traffic across ASG instances in multiple AZs.
Common mistake
If bootstrapping takes too long, ELB health checks may mark instances unhealthy before they finish configuration. Keep critical steps fast or use warm pools to reduce disruption.

screens.title: ALB and ASG setup & verification steps
screens.narratorSegment: This practical flow shows the essential steps to create a resilient web deployment: create a target group for HTTP on port 80, create an Application Load Balancer spanning at least two Availability Zones, and create an Auto Scaling Group using your launch template that registers instances with the target group. Health checks must be configured on the target group so the ALB can mark targets healthy or unhealthy. When instances fail a health check, ASG should remove and replace them. Verification should include three checks: load distribution, health-based routing, and ASG replacement. To verify distribution, open the ALB DNS name and refresh several times; you should see responses from different instance IDs. For health-based routing, intentionally make one instance unhealthy (for example, stop the web server) and confirm the ALB stops routing to it. For ASG replacement, terminate an ASG-managed instance and observe that the ASG launches a replacement matching the launch template. Step-by-step

Misconception

Don’t assume regional failover will be instant. Use tested procedures and automation for cross-Region recovery.

screens.title: Identifying & mitigating single points of failure
screens.narratorSegment: A single point of failure is any component whose failure stops the entire system from working. To find SPOFs, review each architectural layer: compute, storage, database, networking, and third-party integrations. Start with compute: a single EC2 instance running critical services without an ASG is a SPOF. Replace it with an ASG and distribute instances across AZs. For storage, rely on managed services with built-in replication like Amazon S3 or RDS Multi-AZ instead of single-instance storage. For networking, avoid single NAT gateways or single Internet-facing proxies; provision redundant NAT gateways and route tables across AZs. Databases are frequent SPOFs; use RDS Multi-AZ or read-replicas with cross-AZ failover depending on your consistency needs. Third-party integrations — SaaS dependencies or on-premises VPN links — can also be SPOFs; consider alternatives or circuit breakers to degrade gracefully. Always ask: what happens if this component fails? Then apply redundancy, failover, or graceful degradation. Test your mitigations with failure drills: terminate instances, disable AZs in simulations, and run recovery procedures. The key insight is that redundancy must be end-to-end. Adding redundancy in one layer while leaving another single-threaded still leaves the system vulnerable.

Compute

Database

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: These are the core ideas to keep front of mind. First, high availability reduces downtime through redundancy and fast recovery while fault tolerance aims to keep systems running uninterrupted despite component failures. Second, Availability Zones and Regions are the physical foundation: distribute resources across AZs for local resilience and use multi-Region only when you need protection against regional disasters. Third, Elastic Load Balancing and Auto Scaling Groups work together to route traffic to healthy targets and replace failed instances automatically — but they only help if instances are stateless or state is externalized. Finally, choose a disaster recovery strategy that aligns with your RTO and RPO targets and test it regularly; untested DR is effectively no DR. Keep asking what fails when a component stops and design redundancy accordingly. These principles apply whether you’re deploying a small web app or a mission-critical service.

screens.title: What to Remember
screens.narratorSegment: Keep these quick reminders handy as you design resilient systems. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we focus on practical patterns that keep applications running when things fail. You will learn the difference between high availability and fault tolerance, and why both matter when architecting for production workloads. We will explore how Availability Zones and Regions form the physical foundation of resilience, and how services like Elastic Load Balancing and Auto Scaling create self-healing front doors and horizontally scaled fleets. You will also walk through common disaster recovery strategies — backup and restore, pilot light, warm standby, and multi-site active/active — and learn to match each to Recovery Time Objectives and Recovery Point Objectives. Finally, we will highlight typical single points of failure you must eliminate, such as single-instance databases or missing cross-AZ replication, and the simple changes that reduce risk. By the end of this lesson you will be able to propose a multi-AZ design for a simple web application, choose an appropriate DR pattern for business requirements, and identify where redundancy is missing. Think about a legacy app you know: how quickly could it recover from an AZ outage, and what would you change first?

By the end of this chapter you will do four practical things that improve system resilience. First, you will clearly explain how high availability differs from fault tolerance and why both are needed for critical services. Second, you will design multi-Availability Zone and multi-Region layouts that reduce the blast radius of failures and support business continuity. Third, you will configure and reason about Application Load Balancers and Auto Scaling Groups so your application can route around unhealthy instances and replace failed capacity automatically. Fourth, you will choose and justify a disaster recovery pattern — backup and restore, pilot light, warm standby, or multi-site active/active — based on Recovery Time Objective and Recovery Point Objective targets. Each objective focuses on practical decision-making and hands-on skills that map directly to real AWS deployments and exams. As you progress, think about which objective you would practice first on a test application and why.

This second objectives slide shifts from theory to practice. You will design a Launch Template for EC2 with user data to provision a web server, create a target group and Application Load Balancer that spans at least two Availability Zones, and configure an Auto Scaling Group with health checks so instances are replaced automatically. You will verify behavior by exercising the ALB DNS name and by terminating instances to observe ASG healing. These activities build intuitive understanding: watching an instance fail and be replaced makes fault tolerance tangible. A common misconception is that simply placing multiple instances in the same AZ equals resilience — it does not. True resilience requires distributing capacity across independent AZs and using managed services that route, monitor, and heal. Practice these steps on a small test application first to see the impact without risking production traffic.

High availability and fault tolerance are related goals but they are not the same. High availability focuses on keeping a system operational for a long time and is often expressed as an uptime percentage — for example, 99.99 percent availability. Achieving HA means designing to reduce downtime through redundancy, fast detection, and quick recovery. Fault tolerance is a stronger claim: the system continues operating without interruption even when one or more components fail. True fault-tolerant systems mask failures so users notice no downtime at all. In practice you choose a mix: multi-AZ deployments and load balancers provide high availability by keeping services running despite component failures, while synchronous replication and active/active multi-Region architectures approach fault tolerance by eliminating single failure modes. A common misconception is that adding more instances alone guarantees fault tolerance. It does not unless you also eliminate correlated failure modes like a single database or single NAT gateway. Example: deploying two identical web servers in a single AZ behind a load balancer improves availability against instance failure, but won’t protect you if the AZ loses power. The takeaway: map business availability targets to design choices and then remove single points of failure methodically.

Regions and Availability Zones are the physical building blocks for resilience on AWS. A Region represents a geographic area containing multiple isolated AZs. An AZ is one or more discrete data centers with independent power and networking. Because AZs within a Region are interconnected using high-bandwidth, low-latency links, you can run multi-AZ architectures that replicate data and route traffic between AZs quickly. Deploying application tiers — web, application, and database — across multiple AZs reduces the impact of a single data center failure. For example, running two web server instances in different AZs behind an Application Load Balancer means the ALB will route traffic to the healthy instance if the other AZ fails. Extending resilience across Regions protects against larger disasters, but introduces replication complexity and possible cross-Region latency. A practical trade-off is to use multi-AZ within a Region for typical HA needs and reserve multi-Region designs for critical services with near-zero RTO requirements. Misconception: AZs are backups of each other; they are independent sites and require explicit replication or multi-AZ managed services to replicate state. Consider where to place stateful components and prefer managed multi-AZ options when possible.

Elastic Load Balancing provides managed entry points that distribute traffic to multiple targets and remove unhealthy targets automatically. There are three primary types. Application Load Balancer is optimized for HTTP and HTTPS and supports path-based routing, host-based routing, and advanced request processing. Use ALB when you need layer 7 features for web applications. Network Load Balancer operates at layer 4 and is designed for extreme performance and low latency for TCP, UDP, or TLS traffic. It preserves source IP and is a good fit for performance-sensitive or non-HTTP workloads. Gateway Load Balancer is used for routing traffic to third-party virtual appliances, like firewalls, without changing your networking. Health checks are critical: ELB will detect an unhealthy instance and stop sending traffic to it, preventing requests from hitting failed nodes and eliminating the load balancer itself as a single point of failure. A common misconception is that the presence of a load balancer alone fixes stateful backend issues; it only routes and checks health. If your backend stores state locally on instances, replacing an instance won't restore state. Example: use ALB with an ASG and stateless web servers that store session state in a shared cache or database. The key takeaway: pick the right balancer type and use health checks plus stateless designs to reap HA benefits.

Auto Scaling Groups maintain the desired number of instances for a logical group and provide self-healing behavior. An ASG watches instance health using ELB or EC2 health checks and will terminate and replace instances that fail. Scaling policies — scheduled, simple, or target-tracking — allow ASGs to respond to demand changes automatically. The typical process is: define a launch template or launch configuration that contains the AMI, instance type, and user data; create an ASG with desired/min/max capacity and configure health checks; attach the ASG to a target group on an Application Load Balancer so ELB health checks can inform ASG decisions. Example: set desired capacity to two across two AZs and attach an ALB. If C P U spikes, target tracking can scale out to meet load. If an instance becomes unhealthy, the ASG terminates it and launches a replacement using the same launch template, preserving desired capacity and reducing manual intervention. Common misconception: ASG protects only compute, not configuration drift. Ensure your launch template contains all bootstrapping (user data or configuration management) so replacements are identical. The practical takeaway is to treat ASG as the fundamental mechanism for horizontal resilience and combine it with stateless services and externalized state for fast recovery.

Disaster recovery strategies trade cost and complexity for lower Recovery Time Objective and Recovery Point Objective. RTO is the maximum acceptable delay to restore service after an outage; RPO is the maximum acceptable amount of data loss measured in time. The simplest DR approach, Backup and Restore, periodically saves data and recreates environments when needed. It has high RTO and RPO — recovery can take hours or longer and recent data may be lost. Pilot Light keeps a minimal set of core services and replicated data running in a DR Region. It reduces RTO and RPO because only full capacity needs to be scaled up after a disaster. Warm Standby maintains a scaled-down but functional environment that can be quickly scaled to production capacity, lowering RTO/RPO further at higher cost. Multi-Site Active/Active runs the application in multiple Regions simultaneously, often providing near-zero RTO and RPO but incurring the highest cost and complexity for data consistency and traffic routing. Example decision: if your business requires recovery within a few hours and can tolerate limited recent data loss, Pilot Light is cost-effective. If you need continuous operation with minimal data loss, invest in active/active. Always test your chosen strategy — untested DR is not a plan. Run drills, measure actual RTO/RPO, and adjust architecture and runbooks accordingly.

Bootstrapping instances with user data is essential so Auto Scaling Group replacements come online healthy and consistent. The user data script installs and starts Apache, enables the service, and writes a simple web page that includes the instance ID and Availability Zone — a helpful verification step. In this example the script updates packages, installs the web server, starts it, and writes an index. html that prints the instance metadata for the instance ID and AZ. A common mistake is to omit error handling or assume network access during boot. If a package repository is unreachable, the instance will be unhealthy. Also, long-running bootstrap steps can delay health checks; prefer fast, idempotent scripts and pull large assets from a pre-baked AMI when possible. Example verification: after ASG launches instances across two AZs, visit the ALB DNS and refresh to observe different instance IDs and AZs in the page. This demonstrates that instances are provisioned correctly and that the ALB distributes traffic. Keep your launch template immutable so replacement instances use the same bootstrapping behavior consistently. Launch Template user-data (bootstrapping) means put repeatable provisioning in user data or a baked ami so asg replacements are consistent and pass health checks quickly.. In practical terms, use user-data to provision a simple apache web server for asg instances. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.
